y="354.5">3</text></g></svg>
      </figure>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>Networks and introductions (24 of 48):</strong> clients, referrals, word of mouth and advice came through peers, friends and family, work contacts, a banker they already knew, and introductions through friends of friends, rather than formal channels.</li>
        <li><strong>A program, event or grant scheme helped (18 of 48):</strong> people credited local programs, events and grants, often for the network they built.</li>
        <li><strong>A mentor made the difference (12 of 48):</strong> a mentor, coach or advisory board built confidence and skills, helped test the idea with customers, or opened doors to investors.</li>
        <li><strong>Grants and other money that does not have to be paid back (10 of 48):</strong> grants were used or wanted, with a wish for early funding of this kind.</li>
        <li><strong>Legal and accounting basics (10 of 48):</strong> introductions to trusted attorneys and accountants, borrowed templates and help with payroll got the business set up.</li>
        <li><strong>Learned on their own (6 of 48):</strong> research, trial and error and online tools instead of programs.</li>
        <li><strong>Seeking money went badly (5 of 48):</strong> a bank deferred or declined, applications were not selected, or investors were unwilling.</li>
        <li><strong>Finding first customers or pilots (3 of 48):</strong> landing a first customer, client or pilot was named as the hardest and most important step, with a wish for established businesses to pilot new products.</li>
        <li><strong>Did not know what to ask (3 of 48)</strong> and <strong>pricing and sales to grow (fewer than 3 of 48):</strong> rare in writing, though the multiple-choice answers on the next step point the same way.
        Two points came up in fewer than 3 of 48 answers each: finding cofounders or business partners, and preferring to stay outside the local business scene.</li>
      </ul>
      <p>We do not split the themes by gender, because subtracting the women's and men's counts from the total would reveal the answers of the 1 person who did not give a gender.</p>
    </div>
  </details>

  <details class="card" id="survey-supporters">
    <summary><span class="card-headline">Supporters on why women raise less funding</span> <span class="card-figure">12 answers</span></summary>
    <div class="card-body">
      <p>People in a supporter role were asked why women entrepreneurs raise less funding than men, and what could help.
        12 of the 17 in that role answered.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-10" id="fnref-10-7" aria-label="Source 10">10</a></sup>
        The question states the funding gap as a starting point, which may shape the answers.</p>
      <ul>
        <li>Bias, including a perception that men build scalable companies and women build solo service businesses, and a preference for tech startups: 6 of 12.</li>
        <li>Women ask or negotiate less, have less confidence or take fewer risks: 4 of 12.</li>
        <li>Childcare and healthcare: 3 of 12.</li>
        <li>Women's time and load: 3 of 12.</li>
        <li>Cultural and gender-role expectations: fewer than 3 of 12.</li>
      </ul>
      <p>5 of the 12 answers suggest a remedy.
        Two came up 3 times each: more women visible in pitch events, panels and classrooms, as mentors, as local success stories or as investors; and support with childcare and healthcare.
        More women investors came up in fewer than 3 of the 12 answers.</p>
    </div>
  </details>

  <h3 id="survey-quotes">In their words</h3>
  <p>Short extracts from written answers, quoted exactly.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-11" id="fnref-11-1" aria-label="Source 11">11</a></sup></p>
  <figure class="quote"><blockquote><p>&ldquo;&hellip;I didn't know what I didn't know and I spent a long time asking the wrong questions.&rdquo;</p></blockquote></figure>
  <figure class="quote"><blockquote><p>&ldquo;I have some great mentors, but most just say "good job, keep going......." they really don't have the connections that I need in the industry.&rdquo;</p></blockquote></figure>
  <figure class="quote"><blockquote><p>&ldquo;I leaned often on my network to try to find new work or clients.&rdquo;</p></blockquote></figure>
  <figure class="quote"><blockquote><p>&ldquo;First customers are the most difficult but the most important&hellip;&rdquo;</p></blockquote></figure>
  <figure class="quote"><blockquote><p>&ldquo;Until we have more women investors, we won't see as many women comfortable with pitching to investors.&rdquo;</p></blockquote></figure>
  <p>Team members' conversations with women who launched startups in Lincoln in the 2010s pointed the same way: they did not know what they did not know, felt alone and unconnected, and had no idea what funding was available.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-85" id="fnref-85-1" aria-label="Source 85">85</a></sup></p>

  <h3 id="survey-limits">Read with care</h3>
  <details class="card" id="survey-limits-card">
    <summary><span class="card-headline">What this survey can and cannot tell us</span> <span class="card-figure">a pilot, not an estimate</span></summary>
    <div class="card-body">
      <ul>
        <li>It reached the team's own contacts, mostly people already inside Lincoln's startup scene, not a random sample of Lincoln founders.</li>
        <li>There were 48 responses, and most questions were answered by 32 to 40 of them; one more answer can move a figure noticeably.</li>
        <li>The groups of women and men are small, so no difference between them here can be called a gender difference.</li>
        <li>The figures include one test entry made by the team and one partial response.</li>
        <li>Written answers were grouped into themes with the help of an AI assistant (Claude Code, using Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 model), first with one coder per answer; a second, independent coding of every answer (same model, without seeing the first codes) agreed on 146 of 160 answers, and the counts shown come from the second coding, with a code for finding first customers added.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-10" id="fnref-10-8" aria-label="Source 10">10</a></sup></li>
        <li>Theme counts use everyone as the base, including people who wrote nothing, so they undercount.</li>
        <li>To protect individuals, counts of 1 or 2 read "fewer than 3", some cells are held back, and some breakdowns by gender are not shown.</li>
      </ul>
    </div>
  </details>
</section>

<p class="note to-top"><a href="#jsr-top">Back to top</a></p>
<section id="rest" class="page-section" aria-labelledby="rest-heading">
<h2 id="rest-heading">The rest of the research</h2>
<p class="section-intro">Beyond the figures in our pitch, we logged about 300 sources on women business owners, capital, mentoring and programs.
Here are the key findings, grouped by topic.
Each card shows the headline first; open it for the detail, how strong the evidence is, and the source.
Most of this evidence is national or from other countries; where it is about Nebraska or Lincoln, the card says so.
Sources already covered in "Research cited in the pitch" are pointed to rather than repeated.</p>

<section class="topic" id="rest-capital" aria-labelledby="rest-capital-heading">
<h3 id="rest-capital-heading">Capital: loans, grants and investment</h3>

<details class="card" id="rest-capital-ladder">
<summary>Nebraska lenders cover loans from <strong>$1,000</strong> to <strong>$5 million</strong>, but nothing lays them out as one path<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">12</sup></summary>
<p>A Lincoln owner can find 0% Kiva loans ($1,000 to $15,000), SBA microloans through Community Development Resources ($1,000 to $50,000), the Nebraska Enterprise Fund ($1,000 to $150,000), Center for Rural Affairs loans ($1,000 to $250,000) and SBA 504 loans through NEDCO for buildings and equipment (up to $5 million).<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-12" id="fnref-12-1" aria-label="Source 12">12</a></sup>
None of the pages we read sets these out as a route by business stage or size, so an owner has to work out for herself which one fits.</p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> loan terms are what each lender states on its own website, read in November 2026.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-capital-women-specific">
<summary>Only <strong>one</strong> women-specific source of capital found in Nebraska: a crowdfunding portal for raises of <strong>$150,000 to $5 million</strong><sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">13</sup></summary>
<p>AeQuitas Invest (AQi), based in Omaha, hosts only companies that are at least 50% women-owned, raising $150,000 to $5 million a year through regulated crowdfunding.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-13" id="fnref-13-1" aria-label="Source 13">13</a></sup>
Almost every other Nebraska source of capital we found is open to everyone, not aimed at women.
Repeated searches found no women's angel group, women-led fund, women's grant or women's pitch competition in Nebraska.</p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> "not found" after several searches in November 2026, not proof that none exists.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-capital-not-applying">
<summary><strong>78%</strong> of women-owned employer firms did not apply for new credit in 2024<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">4</sup></summary>
<p>In the Census Bureau's national survey, 13% of women-owned businesses with employees applied for new credit in 2024, 78% did not, and 9% did not know.
Of those that applied, 53% got all they asked for, 28% some and 8% none.
Community development lenders (CDFIs) supplied credit to only about 1% of those that got it.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-4" id="fnref-4-2" aria-label="Source 4">4</a></sup></p>
<p>This points to not applying, rather than being turned down, as a large part of the story.
The source gives no figure for men-owned firms to compare.</p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> national federal survey, preliminary estimates; no Nebraska figure was checked.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-capital-risk-sharing">
<summary>When a development bank shared lenders' risk, women's share of business lending rose by about <strong>23%</strong><sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">14</sup></summary>
<p>In Türkiye, a development bank lent to five commercial banks on condition they lent on to women-led small businesses, covered first losses up to 10% of each bank's portfolio, and trained bank staff.
In two years, participating banks raised women's share of their business lending by 2 percentage points on average, a rise of almost a quarter from a base of about 9%.
Half of the rise came from new borrowers, and first-time women borrowers were as likely to repay as others.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-14" id="fnref-14-1" aria-label="Source 14">14</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> a careful before-and-after comparison using the national credit registry, read in the bank's four-page brief; the brief does not separate the effect of the risk cover from the credit lines and training.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-capital-loan-design">
<summary>Changing loan terms changed results for women: a <strong>two-month</strong> repayment grace period raised long-run profits, and also defaults<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">15</sup></summary>
<p>In a trial in India, giving women borrowers two months before their first repayment led to more business investment and higher long-run profits, but more of them defaulted.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-15" id="fnref-15-1" aria-label="Source 15">15</a></sup>
In a small trial in Ethiopia, judging loan applications on a psychometric test instead of fixed collateral improved women's access to credit and their businesses' survival, with little sign of growth.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-16" id="fnref-16-1" aria-label="Source 16">16</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> both are randomised trials outside the US.
The India result was read at abstract level.
For Ethiopia we give only the direction of the effect, because the draft that holds the figures asks not to be cited.</p>
</details>
</section>

<section class="topic" id="rest-networks" aria-labelledby="rest-networks-heading">
<h3 id="rest-networks-heading">Networks and mentoring</h3>

<details class="card" id="rest-networks-kenya">
<summary>A local mentor raised women's business profits by about <strong>20%</strong>, but only while the pair kept meeting<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">17</sup></summary>
<p>In Kenya, women running small businesses who were paired with an experienced local businesswoman raised their profits by about 20%, while a business class did not help.
The gains faded as pairs stopped meeting, and lasted for pairs still meeting after a year.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-17" id="fnref-17-1" aria-label="Source 17">17</a></sup>
In an earlier version of the study, 45% of pairs were still meeting after twelve months, and mentees said nearly 70% of the matches that ended were ended by the mentor.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-17" id="fnref-17-2" aria-label="Source 17">17</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> randomised trial with 372 women, outside the US.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-networks-mentor-gender">
<summary>Women mentored by women in Uganda raised sales <strong>32%</strong> and profits <strong>31%</strong>; a second trial points the other way<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">18</sup></summary>
<p>In one trial, women entrepreneurs mentored remotely by a woman raised sales 32% and profits 31%, while women mentored by a man did not improve significantly; mentor gender made no difference for men.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-18" id="fnref-18-1" aria-label="Source 18">18</a></sup>
The women-with-women group was small: 48 in the final analysis.</p>
<p>A second Uganda trial, of group mentoring on top of a cash grant, found mentoring did not help women overall.
Its draft brief reports lower profits for women in all-women groups with a woman mentor, while its full paper finds no significant difference between men and women mentors for women.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-19" id="fnref-19-1" aria-label="Source 19">19</a></sup>
The two trials differ in design (one-to-one and remote against group mentoring with cash), so they are best read as disagreeing, not as one cancelling the other.</p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> two randomised trials, both outside the US, with different results.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-networks-getting-matched">
<summary>Signing up is not being mentored: only <strong>27%</strong> of surveyed users of an online mentoring platform had received mentoring<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">20</sup></summary>
<p>In a 2020 evaluation of MicroMentor, 27% of 894 surveyed entrepreneurs had been mentored.
Among those who had not, 28% said a mentor never replied and 23% did not know how to contact one.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-20" id="fnref-20-1" aria-label="Source 20">20</a></sup>
In a UK survey, 39% of small firms that had never used a mentor did not know where they would find one.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-21" id="fnref-21-1" aria-label="Source 21">21</a></sup>
The randomised trial on the same platform that our pitch cites found the same bottleneck; see <a href="#cited-mentoring-trial">Research cited in the pitch</a>.</p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> an evaluation commissioned by the platform's funder, mostly of users in developing countries, and a UK government survey of 902 firms; observational.
The report is not consistent on whether the 28% and 23% are shares of users who had not been mentored or of all surveyed users.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-networks-groups">
<summary>Group formats can match one-to-one help at lower cost: group consulting cost about <strong>a third</strong> as much per firm<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">22</sup></summary>
<p>In Colombia, consulting delivered to groups of firms raised sales, profits and productivity at about a third of the cost of one-to-one consulting (US$10,500 against US$28,950 per firm), whose effects were weaker.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-22" id="fnref-22-1" aria-label="Source 22">22</a></sup>
In China, monthly meetings among small groups of business owners, with no mentor, raised revenue 8%, and the gain lasted a year after the meetings ended.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-23" id="fnref-23-1" aria-label="Source 23">23</a></sup>
In Kenya, mentoring added to a cash grant only marginally improved results, and cash alone cost less per dollar of extra profit (US$3.43 against US$4.56).<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-19" id="fnref-19-2" aria-label="Source 19">19</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> randomised trials outside the US; the Kenya cash result is from a draft research brief.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-networks-sparing-mentors">
<summary>Mentors' time is the scarce resource: SCORE, a national volunteer mentoring network, asks for <strong>10 to 12 hours</strong> a month and caps new requests each week<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">24</sup></summary>
<p>SCORE asks mentors for 10 to 12 hours a month, lets them pause for up to 30 days, and since November 2025 limits how many new requests each mentor receives a week, hiding mentors who have reached their limit.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-24" id="fnref-24-1" aria-label="Source 24">24</a></sup>
How programs back their volunteers matters too: on one online platform, corporate-recruited mentors given intensive support did well, while those given only light support did worse than those given none at all (2,344 mentors).<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-25" id="fnref-25-1" aria-label="Source 25">25</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> SCORE's rules are its own published procedures, with no data on whether they keep mentors longer; the platform study is observational.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-networks-lincoln">
<summary>Lincoln has several pools of mentors, but few published counts: SCORE reports <strong>61</strong> volunteers across Nebraska<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">26</sup></summary>
<p>SCORE has two Nebraska chapters, Lincoln and Greater Omaha, with 61 volunteers statewide in its 2024 figures; no Lincoln-only count was found.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-26" id="fnref-26-1" aria-label="Source 26">26</a></sup>
The University of Nebraska-Lincoln reports mentors supporting student entrepreneurs rising from 165 to 252 in one year, all for UNL students.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-27" id="fnref-27-1" aria-label="Source 27">27</a></sup>
NMotion, Lincoln's accelerator, takes six companies per cohort.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-28" id="fnref-28-1" aria-label="Source 28">28</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> each organisation's own figures, not independently checked.</p>
</details>
</section>

<section class="topic" id="rest-models" aria-labelledby="rest-models-heading">
<h3 id="rest-models-heading">Program models elsewhere</h3>

<details class="card" id="rest-models-10ksb">
<summary>A free growth program for established owners: <strong>57%</strong> of graduates reported adding jobs within 30 months<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">29</sup></summary>
<p>Goldman Sachs 10,000 Small Businesses teaches owners of existing businesses to plan for growth.
In its 2018 impact report, 45% of participants were women, and 57% of alumni reported adding jobs at 30 months, against 25% of small businesses in a national survey used as a benchmark.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-29" id="fnref-29-1" aria-label="Source 29">29</a></sup>
It is free to participants, and it now accepts applicants from Omaha through a regional cohort.</p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> self-reported follow-up surveys; no randomised or matched comparison group, and no results by gender.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-models-uk-code">
<summary>In the UK, investors who report founder gender backed teams with a woman founder in <strong>33%</strong> of deals, against <strong>25%</strong> in the wider market<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">30</sup></summary>
<p>The UK's Investing in Women Code asks investors and lenders to report each year who they fund.
By March 2026 it had 337 signatories.
In 2025, 33% of signatories' venture deals went to teams with at least one woman founder, against 25% in the wider market, and community lenders that signed made 37% of their business loans to women-led firms.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-30" id="fnref-30-1" aria-label="Source 30">30</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> government-published annual figures; firms choose to sign, so the gap does not prove the Code caused it.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-models-wwbic">
<summary>A Wisconsin women's lender: <strong>69%</strong> of its borrowers were still in business after five years, against <strong>50%</strong> nationally<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">31</sup></summary>
<p>The Wisconsin Women's Business Initiative Corporation, founded in 1987, combines small loans with training and coaching.
A third-party study released in 2022 found 69% of its borrowers still in business after five years, against 50% nationally, and 70% of borrowers who came with poor credit improved their score.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-31" id="fnref-31-1" aria-label="Source 31">31</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> compared with population averages, not with similar businesses, and not split by gender.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-models-canada">
<summary>Canada's grants to women-owned firms: <strong>41%</strong> of recipients reported hiring, but support groups stopped when the money ended<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">32</sup></summary>
<p>Canada's Women Entrepreneurship Strategy gave grants of up to C$100,000 to 322 women-owned firms and funded 52 support organisations.
41% of grant recipients reported hiring more staff.
The evaluators found that no new businesses were funded, because two years of accounts were required, and that many support organisations stopped their services when the funding ended.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-32" id="fnref-32-1" aria-label="Source 32">32</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> government evaluation based on recipients' own reports, with no comparison group.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-models-ireland">
<summary>Ireland's development agency went from <strong>1 in 10</strong> to <strong>more than 1 in 3</strong> supported start-ups led by women<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">33</sup></summary>
<p>Enterprise Ireland paired a start-up fund for women-led companies with a women's accelerator from 2012.
By 2017, more than one in three start-ups it supported were led by women, against one in ten in 2012, and 46% of that year's start-fund investments went to women-led companies.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-33" id="fnref-33-1" aria-label="Source 33">33</a></sup>
The women-only fund's last call closed in 2021; a women founders' accelerator continues.</p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> the agency's own figures, which it credits to its targeted programs; not an independent evaluation.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-models-care">
<summary>A Hawai'i accelerator pays each founder a <strong>$4,000</strong> care stipend; no Nebraska program found pays for childcare<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">34</sup></summary>
<p>Hawai'i FoundHer gives each founder a $20,000 grant and a $4,000 stipend for child or elder care during its six-month program.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-34" id="fnref-34-1" aria-label="Source 34">34</a></sup>
We found no program in Nebraska, or any national online program, that pays for or provides childcare for founders; Nebraska programs fit around caregiving, if at all, through online or part-time formats.</p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> program terms from its website; the absence in Nebraska is "not found" in our searches.</p>
</details>
</section>

<section class="topic" id="rest-evidence" aria-labelledby="rest-evidence-heading">
<h3 id="rest-evidence-heading">Evidence on the funding gap</h3>

<details class="card" id="rest-evidence-approval">
<summary>Once women-owned firms apply for a loan, the approval gap is small and changes direction: <strong>49%</strong> against <strong>52%</strong> got the full amount in 2025<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">5</sup></summary>
<p>In the Federal Reserve's national survey of businesses with employees, the share of women-owned firms that got the full amount they applied for was 49% in 2025 (men-owned 52%), 54% in 2024 (men-owned 50%) and 45% in 2022 (men-owned 55%).<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-5" id="fnref-5-2" aria-label="Source 5">5</a></sup>
The larger gaps sit earlier: in having employees at all (see <a href="#cited-hiring">Research cited in the pitch</a>) and in applying at all (see the capital cards above).</p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> large national survey, read from the Federal Reserve's own data series; there is no Nebraska breakdown.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-evidence-women-investors">
<summary>More women writing checks moved money to women founders; persuading men did not<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">6</sup></summary>
<p>After a high-profile 2015 lawsuit, US venture firms hired more women investors, and the share of funded founders who were women rose.
The rise was "driven entirely by the hiring of female venture capitalists"; male investors did not become more likely to back women.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-6" id="fnref-6-2" aria-label="Source 6">6</a></sup>
On an online investing platform where every investor saw the same profiles, women-led startups did less well with male investors and better with female investors.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-35" id="fnref-35-1" aria-label="Source 35">35</a></sup>
Women were 39% of active US angel investors in 2024, according to the angel market report also used in <a href="#cited-angels">Research cited in the pitch</a>.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-3" id="fnref-3-3" aria-label="Source 3">3</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> two US studies, a journal article read through its authors' summary and a working paper read at abstract level; both observational. The 39% is the angel report's own count.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-evidence-questions">
<summary>Investors ask men about gains and women about risks; startups asked mostly about gains raised <strong>$16.8 million</strong> on average, against <strong>$2.3 million</strong><sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">36</sup></summary>
<p>At a major US startup competition (189 startups, 2010 to 2016), investors tended to ask men questions about gains and growth and women questions about risks and losses.
Startups asked mostly about gains raised $16.8 million on average, against $2.3 million, and each extra question about risks meant $3.8 million less, which fully accounted for gender's effect on funding.
In a follow-up experiment, founders who answered risk questions by talking about gains raised more.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-36" id="fnref-36-1" aria-label="Source 36">36</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> peer-reviewed field study plus experiment, US, high-growth tech startups; checked against the published paper.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-evidence-voice">
<summary>With identical pitches, <strong>68%</strong> chose to fund the one narrated by a man<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">37</sup></summary>
<p>In an experiment, 356 of 521 participants (68%) chose to fund the pitch voiced by a man when the words were the same.
In real pitch competitions, male entrepreneurs were 60% more likely to win.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-37" id="fnref-37-1" aria-label="Source 37">37</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> peer-reviewed US study from 2014, so dated; checked against the published paper.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-evidence-cold-email">
<summary>At first contact, investors replied with interest <strong>9%</strong> more often to women<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">38</sup></summary>
<p>In an experiment, 80,000 pitch emails from fictitious founders went to about 28,000 venture investors and angels.
Only 4% got an interested reply, and emails from women got a 9% higher rate of interested replies than identical emails from men.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-38" id="fnref-38-1" aria-label="Source 38">38</a></sup>
So the barrier does not seem to be the first written contact; the evidence points more to who is in the room and how women are received there.</p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> randomised field experiment, US and international investors, 2018; read in the 2019 working paper.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-evidence-loan-officers">
<summary>Loan officers asked for a guarantor <strong>26%</strong> more often when the same application came from a woman<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">39</sup></summary>
<p>In an experiment with 334 loan officers at a large Turkish bank, approval rates did not differ, but officers were 26% more likely to require a guarantor when an identical application came from a woman; the gap sat mostly with young, inexperienced officers.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-39" id="fnref-39-1" aria-label="Source 39">39</a></sup>
At an Albanian microlender, first-time borrowers assigned a loan officer of the other sex paid 38 basis points more a year and were 10% less likely to apply for a second loan.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-40" id="fnref-40-1" aria-label="Source 40">40</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> one randomised and one quasi-random study, both outside the US; the Turkish result read at abstract level.</p>
</details>
</section>

<section class="topic" id="rest-gaps" aria-labelledby="rest-gaps-heading">
<h3 id="rest-gaps-heading">Gaps in what exists</h3>

<details class="card" id="rest-gaps-front-door">
<summary>The rural women's business center that covers Lincoln went from <strong>four</strong> staff to <strong>one</strong><sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">41</sup></summary>
<p>Lincoln's startup hub is framed around startups and names no women's resource, and Nebraska's two women's business centers are based in Omaha and Grand Island.
The Center for Rural Affairs center, whose service area includes Lincoln, had four staff in 2020 and one full-time person in 2026, and two more Nebraska centers announced in January 2025, one for child care businesses, were never funded.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-41" id="fnref-41-1" aria-label="Source 41">41</a></sup>
So there is no Lincoln front door for women who own businesses but do not call themselves founders.</p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> the center's own account; the Lincoln picture comes from our review of local program pages.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-gaps-start-not-grow">
<summary>Women's business centers help people start, not grow: clients' growth and access to capital were <strong>lower</strong> than similar non-clients'<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">42</sup></summary>
<p>The SBA's 2025 evaluation of its women's business centers compared clients with similar businesses that did not use them.
Clients started more businesses, but "business growth outcomes and access to capital declined on average", and businesses they started employed fewer people.
Referrals between centers fell from 28% of clients in 2020 to 8% in 2024.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-42" id="fnref-42-1" aria-label="Source 42">42</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> federal evaluation with a matched comparison group; the evaluators note gaps in their data.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-gaps-training">
<summary>Training alone did not move sales or hiring, even though more than <strong>85%</strong> of trainees called it useful<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">43</sup></summary>
<p>In a US trial with 4,197 applicants, free entrepreneurship training raised business ownership at first, but had no effect on sales or on having an employee, and no lasting effect for women.
More than 85% of trainees said the training was useful.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-43" id="fnref-43-1" aria-label="Source 43">43</a></sup>
Studies of accelerators in mostly developing countries found women-led ventures raised nearly US$100,000 less equity than men-led ones after acceleration<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-44" id="fnref-44-1" aria-label="Source 44">44</a></sup>, and men-led startups raised 2.6 times as much additional equity after acceleration as women-led ones.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-45" id="fnref-45-1" aria-label="Source 45">45</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> one randomised US trial from 2003 to 2005, and one observational and one quasi-experimental study of accelerators outside the US.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-gaps-investor-groups">
<summary>Women's angel groups need a local base: <strong>two</strong> elsewhere closed for lack of members or investors<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">46</sup></summary>
<p>X-Squared Angels in Columbus, Ohio, disbanded at the end of 2018 "as membership fizzled", and Golden Seeds' Philadelphia chapter shut after 2011 because there were not enough local investors.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-46" id="fnref-46-1" aria-label="Source 46">46</a></sup>
We found no women's angel group, angel training or women-led fund in Nebraska.</p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> news reports from 2013 and 2019; the Nebraska absence is "not found" in our searches.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-gaps-data">
<summary>Nebraska publishes almost nothing on capital by owner gender: one figure, <strong>41%</strong> of <strong>17</strong> state-backed deals<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">47</sup></summary>
<p>The only published Nebraska figure we found: of 17 state-backed loans and investments under the federal State Small Business Credit Initiative from August 2022 to December 2023, 41% went to women-owned or controlled businesses.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-47" id="fnref-47-1" aria-label="Source 47">47</a></sup>
The Federal Reserve's small business survey has too few Nebraska responses for a state view.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-48" id="fnref-48-1" aria-label="Source 48">48</a></sup>
A new federal rule will collect owner gender on small business loans, but the first full year of data is due in 2029, and farm lending is left out.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-49" id="fnref-49-1" aria-label="Source 49">49</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> official reports and the federal rule text.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-gaps-legal">
<summary>Programs limited by identity face legal challenge: one grant fund for Black women founders <strong>closed</strong> in 2024<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">50</sup></summary>
<p>The Fearless Fund closed its grant contest for Black women business owners after a 2024 court ruling and settlement, and another grant program paid $125,000 in legal fees to settle a similar suit.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-50" id="fnref-50-1" aria-label="Source 50">50</a></sup>
In October 2025 an interim federal rule removed the transportation contracting program's presumption that women-owned firms are disadvantaged; whether a final rule followed was not checked.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-51" id="fnref-51-1" aria-label="Source 51">51</a></sup>
Any program open only to women would need legal review.</p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> news reports and the federal rule text; this is not legal advice.</p>
</details>
</section>

<section class="topic" id="rest-size" aria-labelledby="rest-size-heading">
<h3 id="rest-size-heading">How big each gap is</h3>

<details class="card" id="rest-size-path">
<summary>Most of the shortfall shows up <strong>before</strong> a woman ever applies for capital</summary>
<p>No source ranks the barriers against each other, and they are measured in different ways, so this is a sense of scale, not a ranking.
Read along the path from owner to funded, hiring company: few women-owned firms have employees (see <a href="#cited-hiring">Research cited in the pitch</a>), and most do not apply for credit (see the capital cards above).
Loan approval shows a small, unstable gap.
Venture capital shows a very large gap in share, but touches few businesses.</p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> our reading of the research, not a single source.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-size-earnings">
<summary>Nebraska men in their own incorporated businesses earn about <strong>1.7 times</strong> what women do<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">52</sup></summary>
<p>In 2023, Nebraska men running their own incorporated businesses earned about $61,507, roughly 1.7 times women's $37,136.
Women were 33% of these business owners.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-52" id="fnref-52-1" aria-label="Source 52">52</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> University of Nebraska Omaha analysis; covers people self-employed in incorporated businesses only.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-size-heartland-vc">
<summary>Women-founded firms in the US heartland got under <strong>0.9%</strong> of US venture capital in 2020<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">53</sup></summary>
<p>Firms with at least one woman founder in 20 heartland states, Nebraska among them, received less than 0.9% of US venture capital in 2020.
Over five years their average deal was $1.7 million, against $3.0 million for women-founded firms nationally.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-53" id="fnref-53-1" aria-label="Source 53">53</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> one analysis of investment data; the 0.9% figure was checked, the deal sizes were not reviewed a second time.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-size-definitions">
<summary>Headline venture figures depend on the definition: <strong>3%</strong> of dollars to women-only teams, <strong>10%</strong> to mixed teams<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">54</sup></summary>
<p>A 2019 count found 3% of venture dollars went to startups founded only by women and 10% to teams of women and men.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-54" id="fnref-54-1" aria-label="Source 54">54</a></sup>
Figures for "at least one woman founder" always run far higher than for all-women teams, so a figure is only comparable with others that use the same definition.
Our challenge packet says all-women teams got about 1% of 2025 US venture dollars; we could not open that source to check it.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-55" id="fnref-55-1" aria-label="Source 55">55</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> the 2019 figures were read on the publisher's page; the 2025 figure is <span class="status status-caution">Not checked</span>.</p>
</details>
</section>

<section class="topic" id="rest-employer" aria-labelledby="rest-employer-heading">
<h3 id="rest-employer-heading">Why women-owned firms stay without employees: choice or constraint?</h3>

<details class="card" id="rest-employer-capital">
<summary>Lower start-up capital is the largest measured reason, about <strong>32%</strong> of the explained gap in having employees<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">56</sup></summary>
<p>In the one large US breakdown we found, measured differences explained about 55% of the gap between women- and men-owned firms in having employees.
Lower start-up capital was the largest single piece (32%), prior work in a similar business added about 7%, and the choice of industry only about 4%.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-56" id="fnref-56-1" aria-label="Source 56">56</a></sup>
The authors cannot say whether lower start-up capital reflects borrowing limits or different plans for the business.</p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> observational, and based on 1992 Census data, so dated.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-employer-start-small">
<summary>Women start with less: <strong>37%</strong> of women-owned firms began with under $5,000, against <strong>30%</strong> of men-owned<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">57</sup></summary>
<p>In 2012, 37% of women-owned firms started with under $5,000 against 30% of men-owned, and 3% started with $100,000 or more against 8%.
Women owners also worked fewer hours in the business: 40% worked under 20 hours a week, against 32% of men.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-57" id="fnref-57-1" aria-label="Source 57">57</a></sup>
Fewer hours do not explain it all: in older data, women's firms were less likely to reach $100,000 in sales at every level of hours.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-56" id="fnref-56-2" aria-label="Source 56">56</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> official Census survey; fewer hours can reflect both preference and caregiving.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-employer-survival">
<summary>Women-owned firms survive as often, but start with <strong>34%</strong> lower revenue and stay smaller<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">58</sup></summary>
<p>In bank data on 138,000 firms founded in 2013, women-owned firms were no more likely to close once other traits were held equal, but started with 34% lower revenue and stayed smaller.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-58" id="fnref-58-1" aria-label="Source 58">58</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> observational, from one bank's customers.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-employer-motives">
<summary>Motives differ, but modestly: <strong>60%</strong> of women employer-owners call work-family balance very important, against <strong>54%</strong> of men<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">59</sup></summary>
<p>Among US owners of firms with employees in 2023, women more often called balancing work and family (60% against 54%) and flexible hours (57% against 50%) very important reasons for owning a business, and less often greater income (57% against 65%) or being their own boss (54% against 65%).<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-59" id="fnref-59-1" aria-label="Source 59">59</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> official national survey of owners who already have employees.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-employer-no-split">
<summary>No study found splits the gap into "chose not to grow" and "was held back"; women-owned startups were about <strong>9 points</strong> less likely to make a first hire<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">60</sup></summary>
<p>We searched for a study that separates choice from constraint and found none.
The one study of the step from no employees to a first employee (US startups of 2004) found women-owned startups about 9 percentage points less likely to hire within a year or two, with owner traits held equal; it does not measure motives.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-60" id="fnref-60-1" aria-label="Source 60">60</a></sup>
The measured drivers cut both ways: less start-up capital can mean smaller plans or less access, and fewer hours can mean preference or caregiving.</p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> "searched, nothing found" for a direct split, limited to the searches we ran; the first-hire study is observational.</p>
</details>
</section>

<section class="topic" id="rest-local" aria-labelledby="rest-local-heading">
<h3 id="rest-local-heading">Lincoln and Nebraska in numbers</h3>

<details class="card" id="rest-local-lincoln">
<summary>The Lincoln area has about <strong>12,600</strong> women-owned businesses; <strong>13%</strong> have employees, against <strong>23%</strong> of men-owned<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">2</sup></summary>
<p>In 2023 the Lincoln metro area had about 12,600 women-owned businesses: about 1,600 with employees and about 11,000 without.
13% of them had employees, against 23% of men-owned businesses, the same pattern as across Nebraska (11% against 22%).
Lancaster County alone gives 13% against 23%.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-2" id="fnref-2-2" aria-label="Source 2">2</a></sup>
So the hiring gap in our pitch is not only a rural Nebraska effect.</p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> Census counts; the counts of businesses with employees are survey estimates with about 10% sampling error for Lincoln.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-local-employers">
<summary>Women-owned firms are <strong>21%</strong> of Lincoln-area employers and employ about <strong>11,200</strong> people<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">61</sup></summary>
<p>Of about 7,600 Lincoln-area businesses with employees in 2023, women-owned firms were 21%.
They employed about 11,200 people, against about 52,900 at men-owned firms.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-61" id="fnref-61-1" aria-label="Source 61">61</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> Census survey estimates.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-local-start-rate">
<summary>Nebraskans start businesses at about three quarters of the US rate: <strong>0.27%</strong> of adults a month, against <strong>0.36%</strong><sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">62</sup></summary>
<p>In 2025, 0.27% of Nebraska adults started a business each month, against 0.36% nationally, ranking Nebraska 35th; Nebraska has been below the US rate in every year since 2019.
Firms that do start survive well: 79% survive their first year, 14th among states.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-62" id="fnref-62-1" aria-label="Source 62">62</a></sup>
No state figures are published by gender because state samples are too small.</p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> national indicators built from federal survey and administrative data; rechecked against the data files.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-local-applications">
<summary>New business applications in Lancaster County hit <strong>3,992</strong> in 2025, the most since at least 2005<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">63</sup></summary>
<p>Business applications in Lancaster County rose from 2,435 in 2019 to 3,992 in 2025, the highest in the 2005 to 2025 series, about 12 per 1,000 residents.
Part of the rise reflects a 53-week year in 2025; on a 52-week basis the rise is about 61%.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-63" id="fnref-63-1" aria-label="Source 63">63</a></sup>
These counts are not split by the owner's sex.</p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> Census administrative counts with privacy noise added; per-resident figure and the 52-week adjustment are our arithmetic.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-local-co-owned">
<summary>Nebraska ranked <strong>45th</strong> on businesses owned by women, but <strong>3rd</strong> on businesses owned equally by women and men<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">64</sup></summary>
<p>Among businesses with employees in 2018, 16% in Nebraska were owned by women (45th of 51) and 20% were owned equally by a woman and a man (3rd).<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-64" id="fnref-64-1" aria-label="Source 64">64</a></sup>
Many Nebraska women may run businesses as co-owners, which counts of women-owned firms leave out.</p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> Nebraska Department of Labor summary of Census survey data; covers businesses with employees only; the co-ownership reading is ours.</p>
</details>
</section>

<section class="topic" id="rest-founders" aria-labelledby="rest-founders-heading">
<h3 id="rest-founders-heading">Who becomes a founder</h3>

<details class="card" id="rest-founders-pipeline">
<summary>The gender gap is small at "I intend to start" and widens after: <strong>12%</strong> of US women were starting a business in 2025, against <strong>15%</strong> of men<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">65</sup></summary>
<p>In the US in 2025, 13% of women and 14% of men intended to start a business; 12% and 15% were in the process of starting one; and 6% and 8% owned a new business.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-65" id="fnref-65-1" aria-label="Source 65">65</a></sup>
Each month, 0.28% of women and 0.44% of men who did not own a business started one.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-66" id="fnref-66-1" aria-label="Source 66">66</a></sup>
So women are lost between intending and running a business, not only before intending.</p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> two large national surveys; neither gives figures for Nebraska by gender.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-founders-peers">
<summary>Women are influenced by women: peer groups explain about <strong>half</strong> of the early-career gender gap in starting businesses<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">67</sup></summary>
<p>Following about 213,000 school graduates in Norway, 11% of men and 6% of women did some entrepreneurship in their first five years.
Men were more influenced by men and women by women, and differences in peer groups explained 53% of the gap.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-67" id="fnref-67-1" aria-label="Source 67">67</a></sup>
In Sweden, having an entrepreneur parent raised the chance of becoming one by about 60%, and mothers passed it to daughters more strongly than fathers did.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-68" id="fnref-68-1" aria-label="Source 68">68</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> large observational studies outside the US.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-founders-intention">
<summary>Saying you plan to start is a leaky signal: <strong>63%</strong> of those who did had taken no step a year later<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">69</sup></summary>
<p>In a panel of adults in Austria and Finland, 63% of the 371 people who said they intended to start a business had taken no action a year later.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-69" id="fnref-69-1" aria-label="Source 69">69</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> observational panel outside the US.</p>
</details>
</section>

<section class="topic" id="rest-beliefs" aria-labelledby="rest-beliefs-heading">
<h3 id="rest-beliefs-heading">Common beliefs, checked against the evidence</h3>

<p class="section-intro">These are beliefs that came up in our pilot survey, mostly in supporters' answers on why women raise less funding, each checked against the research.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-10" id="fnref-10-9" aria-label="Source 10">10</a></sup></p>

<details class="card" id="rest-beliefs-start">
<summary>"Fewer women start businesses": true, but the gap is bigger in growing them: women own <strong>37%</strong> of Nebraska businesses outright but <strong>20%</strong> of those with employees<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">1</sup></summary>
<p>Of Nebraska businesses with an owner's sex recorded in 2022, 37% were owned mostly by women, 56% mostly by men and 7% equally by both; counting the equally owned ones, women own 44%.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-1" id="fnref-1-6" aria-label="Source 1">1</a></sup>
Only 11% of women-owned businesses had employees, against 23% of men-owned, so women own about 20% of the Nebraska businesses that employ people.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-1" id="fnref-1-7" aria-label="Source 1">1</a></sup>
Nationally, women also start fewer businesses: each month in 2025, 0.28% of women and 0.44% of men who did not own a business started one.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-66" id="fnref-66-2" aria-label="Source 66">66</a></sup>
The gap is widest among venture-funded startups: 20% of startups worldwide that raised a first funding round in 2019 had a woman among their founders.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-54" id="fnref-54-2" aria-label="Source 54">54</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> Census-based counts for Nebraska and a large national survey for start rates; no start rate by gender is published for Nebraska.
The 37% and the 20% are our arithmetic from the profile's counts (67,994 of 185,360 businesses; 7,494 of about 37,960 with employees).
The venture figure is global and from one database.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-beliefs-risk">
<summary>"Women are more risk-averse": in <strong>54</strong> repeats of one standard risk test, gender differences were tiny once the data were pooled<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">70</sup></summary>
<p>A review of 54 repeats of one laboratory risk test, with about 7,000 people, found gender differences in fewer than 10% of studies, and "negligible in magnitude once all the data are pooled".<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-70" id="fnref-70-1" aria-label="Source 70">70</a></sup>
A re-analysis of 35 studies found men's and women's risk-taking overlapping by more than 80%.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-71" id="fnref-71-1" aria-label="Source 71">71</a></sup>
This is a contested literature: other widely cited reviews report women choosing less risk on average, and we did not read them, so we call the belief overstated rather than wrong.</p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> both reviews read at abstract level; mostly lab experiments with students, not founders.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-beliefs-fear">
<summary>Fear of failure does differ somewhat: <strong>53%</strong> of US women and <strong>46%</strong> of men said it held them back in 2024<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">72</sup></summary>
<p>In the Global Entrepreneurship Monitor's 2024 survey, 53% of US women and 46% of men said fear of failure held them back from starting a business (asked of adults who see good opportunities to start one).<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-72" id="fnref-72-1" aria-label="Source 72">72</a></sup>
GEM's newest women's report finds the gap much smaller among high-potential founders and concludes that "confidence is not the biggest constraint", pointing instead to finance, networks and support.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-65" id="fnref-65-2" aria-label="Source 65">65</a></sup>
GEM's own reports do not fully agree on the US rate, for reasons we could not establish.</p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> large self-reported survey; the figures do not all line up, so read them as a direction, not a precise size.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-beliefs-asking">
<summary>"Women don't ask": women-led firms do apply for bank credit less often, often because they <strong>expect</strong> to be turned down<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">73</sup></summary>
<p>In about 6,000 small firms in 17 countries, women owners were more often discouraged from applying for bank credit where gender bias was higher, while rejection rates and loan terms did not differ.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-73" id="fnref-73-1" aria-label="Source 73">73</a></sup>
In Europe, women-led firms more often held back from applying, as discouraged borrowers and because more relied on their own funds.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-74" id="fnref-74-1" aria-label="Source 74">74</a></sup>
A US study of new founders found being female lowered the chance of asking for financing.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-75" id="fnref-75-1" aria-label="Source 75">75</a></sup>
The often-quoted claim that women apply for jobs only when 100% qualified and men at 60% has no published source behind it.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-76" id="fnref-76-1" aria-label="Source 76">76</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> observational studies; the US study read at abstract level only.
When women do reach investors, they do at least as well; see the cold-email card above and <a href="#cited-angels">Research cited in the pitch</a>.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-beliefs-negotiate">
<summary>"Women negotiate less": we found no study of founders negotiating terms; once women reach angel investors, <strong>27%</strong> of their deals are funded, against <strong>23%</strong> of all deals<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">3</sup></summary>
<p>We found no study that measures how women founders negotiate investment or loan terms; that is a gap in our searches, not evidence either way.
What is measured is asking: in a US panel of people starting businesses, "being female significantly decreases the probability of asking for financing", as in the card above.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-75" id="fnref-75-2" aria-label="Source 75">75</a></sup>
Once women reach investors, they do at least as well: angels funded 27% of women entrepreneurs' deals in 2024, against 23% of all deals,<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-3" id="fnref-3-4" aria-label="Source 3">3</a></sup> and in 80,000 identical cold emails, investors replied with interest 9% more often to women.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-38" id="fnref-38-2" aria-label="Source 38">38</a></sup>
In the room, investors asked women more about risks and men more about gains, which fully accounted for the gender gap in funding at one major US startup competition.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-36" id="fnref-36-2" aria-label="Source 36">36</a></sup>
4 of the 12 supporters who answered our survey said women ask or negotiate less, have less confidence or take fewer risks.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-10" id="fnref-10-10" aria-label="Source 10">10</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> observational studies for asking, the US study read at abstract level only; a randomised field experiment for cold emails; the angel figures are one report's national estimates.
No study of negotiating terms was found in our searches, which were of our own notes, not a full literature search.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-beliefs-mentors">
<summary>"More women mentors and success stories": they help women reach out, but the clearest funding lever is more women writing checks; a role-model video raised women's outreach to mentors by <strong>57%</strong>, not their connections<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">9</sup></summary>
<p>On an online mentoring platform, a short video of a successful mentoring relationship made women 57% more likely to reach out to a mentor (a relative increase), but did not raise their chance of a meaningful exchange.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-9" id="fnref-9-3" aria-label="Source 9">9</a></sup>
In one trial in Uganda, women entrepreneurs did better with a woman mentor;<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-18" id="fnref-18-2" aria-label="Source 18">18</a></sup> a second, of group mentoring on top of a cash grant, found no significant difference between men and women mentors for women, so the two trials disagree.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-19" id="fnref-19-3" aria-label="Source 19">19</a></sup>
In Norway, women were influenced by women: differences in peer groups explained about half (53%) of the early-career gap in starting businesses.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-67" id="fnref-67-2" aria-label="Source 67">67</a></sup>
For funding, the clearest lever is who writes the checks: after US venture firms hired more women investors, the share of founders who were women rose, and male investors did not become more likely to back women.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-6" id="fnref-6-3" aria-label="Source 6">6</a></sup>
In our survey, more women visible in pitch events, panels and classrooms, as mentors, as local success stories or as investors came up in 3 of the 12 supporters' answers; more women investors came up in fewer than 3.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-10" id="fnref-10-11" aria-label="Source 10">10</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> randomised trials for the video and for mentor gender (the mentor trials outside the US, with different results); large observational studies for peers (Norway) and women investors (US, read at abstract level).</p>
</details>
</section>

<section class="topic" id="rest-ai" aria-labelledby="rest-ai-heading">
<h3 id="rest-ai-heading">Women and AI tools</h3>

<details class="card" id="rest-ai-gap">
<summary>Women used generative AI less than men in 17 of 18 surveys; pooled, they had about <strong>20%</strong> lower odds of using it<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">77</sup></summary>
<p>A review of surveys from 2023 and 2024 found women used generative AI less than men in every survey but one; pooling the 12 with enough data, women had about 20% lower odds of using it.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-77" id="fnref-77-1" aria-label="Source 77">77</a></sup>
The reasons most often measured are lower familiarity and lower confidence; even when everyone in a Kenyan study was offered the same chance to learn ChatGPT, women were about 13% less likely to want to.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-77" id="fnref-77-2" aria-label="Source 77">77</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> a review of published surveys, not a quality-rated systematic review.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-ai-owners">
<summary>Among small-business owners the gap is smaller: <strong>17%</strong> of women-owned and <strong>20%</strong> of men-owned firms paid for an AI service by the end of 2025<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">78</sup></summary>
<p>In Chase business-banking data, 17% of women-owned and 20% of men-owned small businesses had paid for at least one AI service by the end of 2025.
The gap was widest among the youngest owners (14% against 20%) and almost nil among the oldest.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-78" id="fnref-78-1" aria-label="Source 78">78</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> observational transaction data from one bank's customers.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-ai-pew">
<summary>US women have nearly caught up on ever using AI chatbots (<strong>47%</strong> against <strong>50%</strong>), but use them less often<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">79</sup></summary>
<p>In February 2026, 47% of US women and 50% of men said they ever use AI chatbots; 20% of women and 27% of men used them daily, and 35% and 40% of employed adults used them for work tasks.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-79" id="fnref-79-1" aria-label="Source 79">79</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> large national probability survey; the earlier year's question was worded differently, so change over time is approximate.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-ai-mentor">
<summary>An AI business mentor may have helped strong businesses by over <strong>15%</strong>, and set weaker ones back by nearly <strong>10%</strong><sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">80</sup></summary>
<p>In a trial with 640 Kenyan entrepreneurs, some were given an AI business mentor on WhatsApp.
On average it did not improve their results; high performers may have gained over 15%, while low performers did "nearly 10% worse", which the authors put down to which advice owners acted on.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-80" id="fnref-80-1" aria-label="Source 80">80</a></sup>
None of the AI next-step tools for founders that we reviewed publishes evidence on whether users got funded, grew, or met the person they were sent to.</p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> randomised trial outside the US; earlier versions of the paper give different figures.</p>
</details>
</section>

<section class="topic" id="rest-community" aria-labelledby="rest-community-heading">
<h3 id="rest-community-heading">Do women owners reinvest in their communities?</h3>

<details class="card" id="rest-community-jobs">
<summary>In the Great Recession, women-owned US firms cut jobs up to <strong>29%</strong> less than men-owned firms<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">81</sup></summary>
<p>Privately held US firms owned by women were less likely to downsize; year-to-year job cuts were as much as 29% smaller, even after allowing for industry, size and profitability.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-81" id="fnref-81-1" aria-label="Source 81">81</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> observational with controls, 2005 to 2009 data; about keeping jobs in a downturn, not hiring locally.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-community-women-workers">
<summary>Women-owned firms employ far more women: <strong>48%</strong> of their full-time workers, against <strong>28%</strong> in men-owned firms<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">82</sup></summary>
<p>Across firms with five or more workers in 168 economies, 48% of full-time workers in women-owned firms were women, against 28% in men-owned firms.
Women-owned firms were smaller, though, adding fewer jobs per firm.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-82" id="fnref-82-1" aria-label="Source 82">82</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> descriptive World Bank survey data, not US-specific and not adjusted for other differences.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-community-bcorp">
<summary>Woman-owned businesses were <strong>more than three times</strong> as likely to certify as B Corps<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">83</sup></summary>
<p>Among 1,251 US firms in B Lab's records, woman-owned businesses were twice as likely to qualify for B Corp certification, which scores social and environmental performance, and more than three times as likely to certify.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-83" id="fnref-83-1" aria-label="Source 83">83</a></sup></p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> read at abstract level; compares firms already known to B Lab, not all US firms.</p>
</details>

<details class="card" id="rest-community-90">
<summary>The popular claim that women reinvest <strong>90%</strong> of their income in their families has no traceable study behind it<sup class="fn" aria-hidden="true">84</sup></summary>
<p>The most specific citation we found points to a US government web page that no longer resolves; no primary study was found, and the claim is about household income, not business owners.<sup class="fn"><a href="#fn-84" id="fnref-84-1" aria-label="Source 84">84</a></sup>
Surveys of owners also find women and men give money and time to charity at similar levels, and we found no study measuring whether women owners hire, buy or bank more locally.</p>
<p><strong>How strong:</strong> no study behind the 90% figure was found, so it should not be relied on.</p>
</details>
</section>
</section>
